intro: A mother lights a lamp before an image of Krishna. A monk in a saffron robe holds out his bowl at dawn. Volunteers at a gurdwara serve a free meal to anyone who walks in. A family in Japan bows at a shrine gate, then lights incense at a Buddhist temple down the hill. Each of these scenes belongs to a tradition that began in South or East Asia.

This unit explores seven of those traditions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto. You will read from their sacred texts, such as the Bhagavad Gita, the Dhammapada, the Analects and the Daodejing. You will see how they answer big questions about suffering, duty, nature and how to treat others. You will also see the variety inside each tradition.

Many of these traditions have deep roots in Chicago, from the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions to the temples and gurdwaras of today. By the end of the unit, you will be able to explain key terms in each tradition's own words, attribute each belief to its tradition and compare them fairly without ranking them.
bigQuestion: How do the traditions of South and East Asia teach people to find freedom, harmony and a good life?

title: South and East Asian Traditions

chapters.title: Hinduism and Buddhism: Dharma, Karma, Awakening
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Hindu and Buddhist traditions explain why people suffer and how a person can find freedom?

story.title: The King Who Carved His Regret
story.kicker: After a bloody war, an Indian emperor did something few rulers do: he said he was sorry, in stone.
paragraphs: In about 261 BCE, the armies of the emperor Ashoka marched into Kalinga, a land on the east coast of India. Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire, which stretched across most of the Indian subcontinent. His soldiers won. The cost was enormous. Ashoka's own words later said that about 100,000 people were killed and about 150,000 were carried away as captives.

Ashoka did not celebrate. Instead, he ordered words carved on rocks and tall stone pillars across his empire. In one of these messages, called Rock Edict XIII, the king says he feels deep sorrow over Kalinga. He writes that the only true conquest is a conquest by dhamma, a word that here means right conduct and moral teaching.

The edicts ask people to respect their parents, to be kind to servants and to animals, and to honor the teachers of every religious group. Ashoka had become a follower of the Buddha's teaching. Yet he urged respect for all sects, not only his own. His messages were written in local languages and scripts so ordinary people could hear them read aloud.

Some of these pillars still stand today. One pillar top, with four lions standing back to back, became the national emblem of modern India. Historians still debate how Ashoka governed after Kalinga. But his carved words remain one of the oldest records of a ruler trying to rule by a moral teaching.
story.think: Why might a powerful king choose to carve his regret in public, where everyone could read it?

lessons.title: The Vedas and the Upanishads
lessons.mainIdea: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures, and the Upanishads within them explore the link between the self and ultimate reality.
reading: Before sunrise in many Hindu homes, someone chants a short verse in Sanskrit called the Gayatri Mantra. It comes from the Rig Veda, one of the oldest texts still used in worship anywhere. Hindus call these texts the *Vedas*, from a Sanskrit word meaning knowledge. There are four Vedas, and many Hindus regard them as revealed truth that ancient sages heard, not wrote.

Scholars date the oldest parts of the Rig Veda to about 1500 to 1200 BCE. For centuries, the Vedas were passed on by memory. Priests trained for years to chant every sound exactly. Only much later were they written down. The Vedas contain hymns to many deities, instructions for fire rituals and, in their later parts, deep questions about life.

Those later parts are the *Upanishads*, composed from about 800 BCE onward. They ask: What is the real self? What is behind all things? Many Upanishads answer that the inner self, called Atman, is one with Brahman, the ultimate reality. Hindu schools of thought read this teaching in different ways, and they still debate it today.

words.d: the four oldest Hindu scriptures, first passed on by memory in Sanskrit
later texts of the Vedas that explore the self and ultimate reality
in Hindu thought, the true inner self

look.title: A Father Teaches His Son
look.text: A father asks his son to put salt into water overnight. In the morning the son cannot find the salt, yet every sip tastes salty. The father explains that the finest essence is present in everything in the same way, unseen. That essence is the true self. And, he tells his son, you are that.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (the teaching of Uddalaka to Shvetaketu), paraphrase
look.prompt: What does the salt stand for in the father's lesson? What is he trying to help his son understand about himself?

check.q: What does the word Veda mean?
check.why: Veda comes from a Sanskrit word for knowledge. Duty is dharma; rebirth is part of samsara.

check.q: How were the Vedas passed on for many centuries?
check.why: Priests memorized and chanted the Vedas exactly; writing came much later. Stone pillars belong to Ashoka.

check.q: What question is at the center of the Upanishads?
choices: the link between the inner self and ultimate reality
check.why: The Upanishads explore Atman, the inner self, and Brahman, ultimate reality.

lessons.title: Two Great Epics
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are long story-poems that teach Hindus about duty through heroes facing hard choices.
reading: Every autumn, in towns across northern India, actors perform the story of Prince Rama. Crowds watch him lose his throne, go into the forest with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana, and rescue Sita from the demon king Ravana. This story is the *Ramayana*, an epic poem traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki. Many Hindus see Rama as an image of perfect duty and honor.

The *Mahabharata* is even longer. Scholars call it one of the longest poems ever composed, with about 100,000 verses in its fullest form. It tells of a great war between two branches of one royal family. Both epics grew over many centuries, roughly between 400 BCE and 400 CE. Today many families know them through retellings, comics and TV series.

Inside the Mahabharata is the *Bhagavad Gita*, or Song of the Lord. Just before battle, the warrior Arjuna does not want to fight his own relatives. His charioteer, Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as a form of God, teaches him. Krishna says Arjuna must do his duty without being attached to the results. Hindus have read this teaching in many ways, and millions study it closely.

words.d: a Hindu epic poem about Prince Rama, Sita and the rescue from Ravana
a very long Hindu epic about a war between two branches of one family
a part of the Mahabharata in which Krishna teaches the warrior Arjuna

look.title: Krishna Speaks to Arjuna
look.text: You have a right to do your work, but not to its fruits. Do not let the reward be your reason for acting, and do not fall into doing nothing. Act with a steady mind, the same in success and failure.
look.prompt: Krishna tells Arjuna to act without being attached to results. How could a student use this idea while studying for a test?

check.q: Who is the hero of the Ramayana?
check.why: The Ramayana tells of Prince Rama. Arjuna is a warrior in the Mahabharata.

check.q: Where is the Bhagavad Gita found?
check.why: The Gita is a section of the Mahabharata, set just before its great battle.

check.q: In the Gita, what does Krishna urge Arjuna to do?
choices: leave home and become a monk
do his duty without clinging to the results
check.why: Krishna teaches action without attachment to its fruits (Gita 2.47).

lessons.title: Brahman and the Deities
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus worship many deities while understanding them as forms or faces of one ultimate reality, Brahman.
reading: Walk into a Hindu temple and you may see many sacred images, called murtis. One shows Ganesha, with an elephant's head, whom many Hindus pray to before starting something new. Another shows Lakshmi, linked with good fortune. Another shows Shiva, dancing in a ring of fire. A visitor might ask: how many gods do Hindus worship?

Hindus answer in different ways. Many describe one ultimate reality, *Brahman*, beyond all names and forms. They see the many *deities* as forms or faces of that one reality. A common saying from the Rig Veda states that truth is one, but the wise call it by many names. Other Hindus focus devotion on one supreme God, such as Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess, called Devi.

Families often have an ishta devata, a chosen deity they feel closest to. Followers of Vishnu are called Vaishnavas. Followers of Shiva are called Shaivas. Followers of the Goddess are called Shaktas. These are not separate religions. They are major paths within Hinduism, and they share many texts, festivals and ideas.

words.d: in Hindu thought, the one ultimate reality behind all things
gods and goddesses who are worshiped
a sacred image of a deity used in Hindu worship

look.title: One Reality, Many Names
look.text: A Hindu grandmother keeps a small shrine at home with images of Ganesha, Krishna and Lakshmi. Her grandson asks if she believes in three gods. She says each one shows her a different face of the same divine reality, like one person who is a mother, a teacher and a friend.
look.prompt: Use the words Brahman and deities to explain the grandmother's answer in your own words.

check.q: What is Brahman in Hindu thought?
choices: the one ultimate reality behind all things
check.why: Brahman is the ultimate reality; many Hindus see the deities as its forms.

check.q: A family prays to Ganesha before starting a new business. Why?
choices: Ganesha is the hero of the Ramayana
many Hindus pray to Ganesha before new beginnings
check.why: Many Hindus honor Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity, at the start of new work.

check.q: What is a Vaishnava?
choices: a Hindu whose devotion centers on Vishnu
check.why: Vaishnavas focus devotion on Vishnu; followers of Shiva are Shaivas.

lessons.title: Dharma, Karma, Samsara, Moksha
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu teaching links duty, the results of actions, the cycle of rebirth and the hope of release into one picture of life.
reading: A teenager in Chennai helps care for her grandfather, studies hard and tells the truth even when it costs her. Her family might say she is following her *dharma*. Dharma means duty, or the right way to live. In Hindu teaching, a person's dharma depends partly on their stage of life and role, such as student, parent or elder.

Hindus teach that every action has results that return to the one who acts. This is *karma*. Good actions tend to bring good results; harmful actions bring suffering. Many Hindus believe karma carries across lifetimes. The soul is reborn again and again in a cycle called *samsara*, and karma helps shape each new birth.

The highest goal, many Hindus say, is *moksha*, release from the cycle of rebirth. Hindu paths describe different ways toward moksha. The path of knowledge seeks insight. The path of devotion seeks loving surrender to God. The path of action does one's duty selflessly. Many Hindus combine these paths in daily life.

words.d: duty; the right way to live for one's role and stage of life
the teaching that actions bring results back to the one who acts
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
in Hindu teaching, release from the cycle of rebirth

look.title: Four Words, One Circle
look.text: Picture a wheel. On the rim are the words birth, life, death and rebirth. Arrows labeled karma push the wheel around. A path labeled dharma runs along the rim. At the center, off the wheel, is a doorway labeled moksha.
look.prompt: Explain what each part of the picture stands for in Hindu teaching. Why is moksha drawn off the wheel?

check.q: Which word means the cycle of birth, death and rebirth?
check.why: Samsara is the cycle of rebirth; moksha is release from it.

check.q: A man keeps his promises and cares for his family because it is his duty. Which Hindu idea fits best?
check.why: Dharma is duty or the right way to live.

check.q: What do many Hindus see as the highest goal?
check.why: Many Hindus describe moksha as the final goal beyond samsara.

lessons.title: Puja, Temples and Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu worship happens at home and in temples through offerings, prayers and festivals that bring families together.
reading: In the morning, a mother in Aurora, Illinois, rings a small bell at the family shrine. She offers a flower, lights a lamp and waves it in circles before an image of Krishna. This act of worship is called *puja*. Puja can be simple or grand. It often includes light, flowers, food, incense and prayer.

In a *mandir*, or Hindu temple, priests care for the murtis each day, bathing and dressing them. Worshipers come for darshan, which means seeing and being seen by the deity. The Chicago area has several large temples. The Hindu Temple of Greater Chicago in Lemont and the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora draw families from across the region.

Festivals mark the Hindu year, which follows a lunar calendar. *Diwali*, the festival of lights, comes in October or November. Families light lamps, share sweets and, for many, honor Lakshmi or remember Rama's return home. Holi, in spring, is known for throwing bright colored powder. Other festivals honor Ganesha, Durga and Krishna.

words.d: Hindu worship with offerings such as light, flowers and food
a Hindu temple
the Hindu festival of lights, in October or November

look.title: Where Hindus Live
look.cite: Rounded common estimates from recent census and survey data; estimates vary
look.prompt: About what share of the world's Hindus live in India? What does this tell you about where Hinduism grew?

check.q: What is puja?
choices: worship with offerings such as light and flowers
check.why: Puja is Hindu worship, at home or in a mandir.

check.q: Which festival is known as the festival of lights?
check.why: Diwali is the festival of lights. Holi is the festival of colors; Vesak is Buddhist.

check.q: According to the data, where do most of the world's Hindus live?
check.why: About 1.1 billion Hindus live in India, far more than anywhere else.

lessons.title: Caste: History and Reform
lessons.mainIdea: Caste was a social ranking system in India; many reformers, Hindu and others, worked to end discrimination based on it.
reading: Ancient texts describe four social groups called *varnas*: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, merchants and farmers, and laborers. Over time, society in India also divided into thousands of smaller birth groups called jatis. People often married inside their group and did work linked to it. Scholars call this whole system *caste*.

Some groups were treated as outside the system and called untouchable. They faced harsh exclusion from temples, wells and schools. Many Hindu reformers rejected this treatment, citing the teaching that the same divine self lives in every person. Mahatma Gandhi campaigned against untouchability. Many people today use the name Dalit for these communities.

B. R. Ambedkar, born into a Dalit family, became a lawyer and led the writing of India's Constitution. It took effect in 1950 and outlawed untouchability. In 1956, Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of followers became Buddhists, seeking a path without caste. Discrimination based on caste has not fully disappeared, and Indians still debate how best to end it.

words.d: a system of social groups based on birth, historically linked to work and marriage
one of four broad social groups described in ancient Indian texts
a name many people use for communities once treated as untouchable

look.title: Two Responses to Caste
look.text: Gandhi stayed a Hindu and worked to reform Hindu practice from within, calling for temples to open to everyone. Ambedkar decided that leaving Hinduism for Buddhism was the better path for his followers. Both men wanted to end discrimination based on birth.
look.prompt: Compare the two responses. What did each man believe would bring change? Describe both without judging either.

check.q: What did India's Constitution of 1950 do?
check.why: The 1950 Constitution, led by Ambedkar, outlawed untouchability.

check.q: Why did Ambedkar become a Buddhist in 1956?
choices: he sought a path without caste
he wanted to become a king
check.why: Ambedkar and his followers chose Buddhism as a path free of caste ranking.

check.q: What are jatis?
choices: thousands of smaller birth groups in Indian society
check.why: Jatis are many smaller birth groups; varnas are the four broad groups.

lessons.title: Siddhartha Becomes the Buddha
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist tradition tells how Prince Siddhartha left a life of comfort to seek an end to suffering and became the Buddha, the awakened one.
reading: Buddhist tradition tells of a prince named Siddhartha Gautama, born in Lumbini, in what is now Nepal. Scholars often place his life in the 5th century BCE, though dates vary. His father kept him inside the palace, surrounded by comfort. According to the story, on trips outside he saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a calm wandering holy man.

Troubled, Siddhartha left home to seek an answer to suffering. For years he tried extreme fasting, but it did not bring the answer. He chose a *Middle Way* between luxury and harsh self-denial. Seated under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he meditated until, Buddhists say, he reached awakening. From then on he was called the *Buddha*, which means awakened one.

The Buddha taught for about 45 years across northern India. He gathered a *sangha*, a community of monks and nuns, and lay followers. Buddhists call the Buddha, his teaching (the Dharma) and the Sangha the Three Jewels. Many Buddhists recite that they take refuge in these three.

words.d: the awakened one; the title given to Siddhartha Gautama
the Buddha's path between too much comfort and harsh self-denial
the Buddhist community, especially of monks and nuns

look.title: The First Verse of the Dhammapada
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 1, trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: The Dhammapada is a collection of sayings Buddhists credit to the Buddha. What does this verse say about the power of the mind?

check.q: What does the title Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha means awakened one, the title given to Siddhartha after his awakening.

check.q: What is the Middle Way?
choices: a path between luxury and harsh self-denial
check.why: After trying extreme fasting, Siddhartha chose a Middle Way between extremes.

check.q: Which are the Three Jewels of Buddhism?
choices: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha
the Vedas, the Gita and the Upanishads
check.why: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, his teaching and the community.

lessons.title: Four Truths and an Eightfold Path
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach that suffering has a cause and an end, and that the Eightfold Path is the way to reach that end, called nirvana.
reading: Buddhist tradition says the Buddha's first sermon took place in a deer park near Varanasi. There he taught the *Four Noble Truths*. First, life involves suffering, or dukkha, a word that also means dissatisfaction. Second, suffering comes from craving, which means wanting and clinging. Third, suffering can end. Fourth, there is a path that leads to its end.

That path is the *Eightfold Path*: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Buddhists often group these into three parts: wisdom, ethical conduct and meditation. Here right means wise or skillful, not a rule to obey out of fear.

The goal is *nirvana*, a word that means blowing out, as a flame is blown out. Buddhists describe it as the end of craving and suffering and freedom from rebirth. Like Hindus, Buddhists speak of karma and rebirth. But the Buddha taught that there is no permanent, unchanging self. This is one key point where Buddhist and Hindu teachings differ.

words.d: the Buddha's teaching on suffering, its cause, its end and the path
the eight practices Buddhists follow to end suffering
in Buddhism, the end of craving and suffering and freedom from rebirth

look.title: The First Sermon
look.text: This is the truth of suffering: birth, aging, sickness and death are suffering. This is its cause: craving, which leads to rebirth. This is its ending: the complete fading away of that craving. And this is the path that leads to its ending: the Noble Eightfold Path.
look.cite: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion), Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, paraphrase
look.prompt: Doctors name an illness, find its cause, say whether it can be cured and prescribe a treatment. How does the first sermon follow the same order?

check.q: According to the Four Noble Truths, what causes suffering?
check.why: The Second Noble Truth names craving, or clinging, as the cause of suffering.

check.q: What does nirvana mean literally?
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out, like a flame; duty is dharma and knowledge is veda.

check.q: On which point do Buddhist and Hindu teachings differ?
choices: Buddhists teach there is no permanent self
check.why: Both speak of karma and rebirth, but the Buddha taught no permanent self, while many Hindus speak of Atman.

lessons.title: Ashoka and the Silk Road
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism spread from India across Asia through rulers like Ashoka, monks, pilgrims and traders on the Silk Road.
reading: Ashoka ruled the Mauryan Empire from about 268 to 232 BCE. After the war in Kalinga, he supported the Buddha's teaching. His *edicts*, carved on rocks and pillars, urged kindness, honesty and respect for all religious groups. According to Buddhist tradition, he sent teachers far and wide, and his son Mahinda carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

Over the following centuries, monks and merchants traveled along the *Silk Road*, the network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India. Buddhism reached China by about the 1st century CE. From China it spread to Korea and then to Japan by the 6th century CE. It also traveled by sea to Southeast Asia.

Pilgrims carried texts home. The Chinese monk Xuanzang walked to India in the 600s CE and returned with hundreds of Buddhist texts to translate. In Afghanistan, huge statues of the Buddha were carved into the cliffs at Bamiyan. Each new land shaped Buddhism, blending it with local languages, art and customs.

words.d: an official public order or message from a ruler
a network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India
a person who travels to a holy place for religious reasons

look.title: Ashoka's Regret
look.text: After Kalinga was conquered, the king felt deep sorrow for the killing, death and captivity of so many people. He now holds that the best conquest is conquest by dhamma, and he honors all sects and wishes them to grow in their essential teaching.
look.cite: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (c. 256 BCE), paraphrase
look.prompt: How does Ashoka describe a better kind of conquest? What does he ask of the different religious groups?

check.q: How did Ashoka share his message across his empire?
choices: by carving edicts on rocks and pillars
check.why: Ashoka's edicts were carved on rocks and pillars; the first sermon was the Buddha's.

check.q: What was the Silk Road?
choices: a network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and India
check.why: Monks and traders carried Buddhism along these trade routes.

check.q: Why did Xuanzang travel to India?
choices: to gather Buddhist texts to bring back to China
check.why: The monk Xuanzang brought hundreds of texts back to China to translate.

lessons.title: Theravada, Mahayana and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism grew into major branches, including Theravada and Mahayana, and today Buddhists of many branches live in Chicago.
reading: In Thailand, young men in saffron robes walk barefoot at dawn while families place rice in their bowls. This is *Theravada* Buddhism, meaning the Teaching of the Elders. It is common in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia. Theravada Buddhists use scriptures in the Pali language and give monks a central role.

*Mahayana*, meaning Great Vehicle, spread in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. Mahayana teaching honors the *bodhisattva*, a being who seeks awakening in order to help all others. Mahayana includes Pure Land practice, which centers on devotion to Amida Buddha, and Zen, which stresses meditation. Tibetan Buddhism, sometimes called Vajrayana, is another major tradition.

At Chicago's World's Parliament of Religions in 1893, the Sri Lankan teacher Anagarika Dharmapala spoke for Buddhism. Today the Chicago area has temples of many Buddhist traditions. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago, in Uptown, was founded in 1944 by Japanese Americans. Thai, Vietnamese, Tibetan and Zen communities worship across the city and suburbs.

words.d: the Teaching of the Elders; the Buddhist branch common in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
the Great Vehicle; the Buddhist branch common in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam
in Mahayana Buddhism, a being who seeks awakening to help all others

look.cite: Rounded common estimates of world religious populations; estimates vary
look.prompt: About how many times more Hindus than Buddhists are there? Why might counting Buddhists be harder in countries where people follow more than one tradition?

check.q: Which branch of Buddhism is common in Thailand and Sri Lanka?
check.why: Theravada, the Teaching of the Elders, is the main branch in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

check.q: What is a bodhisattva?
choices: a being who seeks awakening to help all others
check.why: The bodhisattva ideal is central to Mahayana Buddhism.

check.q: Who spoke for Buddhism at Chicago's 1893 Parliament of Religions?
check.why: Dharmapala, from Sri Lanka, represented Buddhism at the 1893 Parliament.

review.q: Which texts are the oldest Hindu scriptures?
review.why: The Vedas, with parts dating to about 1500 BCE, are the oldest Hindu scriptures.

review.q: In the Bhagavad Gita, who teaches Arjuna?
review.why: Krishna, Arjuna's charioteer, teaches him in the Gita.

review.q: Many Hindus describe the deities as forms of what?
review.why: Many Hindus see the deities as faces of Brahman.

review.q: Which pair of ideas do Hindus and Buddhists share?
choices: the Four Noble Truths and the Vedas
review.why: Both traditions speak of karma and rebirth, though they explain them differently.

review.q: What is the goal of the Eightfold Path?
review.why: Buddhists follow the Eightfold Path toward nirvana.

review.q: After the Kalinga war, what did Ashoka call the best conquest?
review.why: In Rock Edict XIII, Ashoka calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest.

review.q: Which branch of Buddhism honors the bodhisattva ideal and includes Zen?
review.why: Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana traditions; Vaishnava and Shaiva are Hindu paths.

review.q: Who led the writing of India's Constitution and later became a Buddhist?
review.why: Ambedkar led the Constitution's drafting and became a Buddhist in 1956.

chapters.title: Sikhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto
chapters.bigQuestion: How do these traditions teach people to live well with others, with nature and with the sacred?

story.title: A Gate, a Bell and One Family
story.kicker: On a Japanese mountain path, one family visits a Shinto shrine and a Buddhist temple on the same day.
paragraphs: Early on New Year's morning, the Sato family climbs a stone path on a hillside in Japan. At the top stands a tall orange gate with two crossbeams, called a torii. It marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine. Before stepping through, the family bows. At a stone basin, they rinse their hands and mouths with a wooden dipper.

At the shrine, each person tosses a coin into a wooden box, rings a bell, bows twice, claps twice and bows once more. Shinto tradition teaches that sacred powers called kami dwell in places like this mountain. The family asks the kami for health and good fortune in the new year. They buy a small charm to hang at home.

Farther down the path is a Buddhist temple. On New Year's Eve, its great bell was struck 108 times. Many Japanese Buddhists say the number stands for 108 worldly desires or troubles. Now the family lights incense there and bows before an image of the Buddha. Later in life, many Japanese families hold funerals with Buddhist rites.

To the Satos, visiting both places on one morning does not feel odd. Many people in Japan take part in both Shinto and Buddhist customs. In China, too, many families have long blended Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist ways. This chapter explores those traditions, and two more from India: Sikhism and Jainism.
story.think: Why might a family feel comfortable taking part in two religious traditions on the same day?

lessons.title: Guru Nanak and the Ten Gurus
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhism began with Guru Nanak in the Punjab, who taught devotion to one God and the equality of all people.
reading: Sikh tradition tells that Guru Nanak, born in 1469 in the Punjab region of South Asia, went to bathe in a river one morning and disappeared for three days. When he returned, he said: There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Sikhs understand this to mean that God sees people beyond such labels. Nanak became the first *Guru*, or teacher, of the Sikhs.

The word Sikh means learner or disciple. Guru Nanak taught that there is one God, the creator, who is present in all creation. He taught that people draw close to God by remembering God's name, working honestly and sharing with others. He rejected ranking people by caste and taught that women and men are equal before God.

Nine more human Gurus followed Guru Nanak, from the 1500s to the early 1700s. The fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, compiled the scripture and built the Harmandir Sahib, known as the Golden Temple, in Amritsar. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, declared before his death in 1708 that the scripture itself would be the Guru from then on.

words.d: a teacher; in Sikhism, the ten founding teachers and the scripture
a learner or disciple; a follower of the Gurus' teaching
the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the most famous Sikh gurdwara

look.title: The Opening of the Sikh Scripture
look.text: There is one Creator. Truth is the divine name. The Creator is without fear and without hatred, timeless, beyond birth and self-existent, known through the Guru's grace.
look.cite: Mul Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib (Japji Sahib), paraphrase
look.prompt: The Mul Mantar opens the Sikh scripture. List three things it says about God. Which idea from Guru Nanak's teaching comes first?

check.q: What does the word Sikh mean?
check.why: Sikh means learner or disciple, a follower of the Gurus.

check.q: Which teaching did Guru Nanak stress?
choices: one God and the equality of all people
check.why: Guru Nanak taught belief in one God and rejected caste ranking.

check.q: What did Guru Gobind Singh declare before his death in 1708?
choices: the scripture would be the Guru
there would be ten more human Gurus
check.why: He named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the lasting Guru.

lessons.title: Scripture, Khalsa and Langar
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as a living Guru, many join the Khalsa, and every gurdwara serves a free shared meal called langar.
reading: In a *gurdwara*, the Sikh house of worship, the *Guru Granth Sahib* rests on a raised platform under a canopy. A reader waves a whisk over it as a sign of respect. Its hymns are written in Gurmukhi script and are sung with music. The book contains hymns by Sikh Gurus and also by Hindu and Muslim holy poets.

In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the *Khalsa*, a community of initiated Sikhs. Members promise to live by Sikh teaching and keep five articles of faith called the five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kara (a steel bracelet), kanga (a wooden comb), kachera (cotton undershorts) and kirpan (a small sword). Many Sikh men and some Sikh women wear a turban to cover their uncut hair.

Every gurdwara has a *langar*, a free community kitchen. Anyone may eat, of any faith or none. Guests traditionally sit together on the floor, so no one sits higher than another. Volunteers cook, serve and wash dishes as seva, or selfless service. The Golden Temple in Amritsar serves many thousands of people every day. Gurdwaras in the Chicago area, such as in Palatine, also serve langar.

words.d: a Sikh house of worship
the Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru
the community of initiated Sikhs founded in 1699
the free shared meal served at every gurdwara

look.title: Sikhs Around the World
look.cite: Rounded common estimates from national census and survey data; estimates vary
look.prompt: Where do most Sikhs live? Which country outside India on this list has the most Sikhs?

check.q: What is langar?
choices: a free shared meal at the gurdwara
check.why: Langar is the free community kitchen; the steel bracelet is the kara.

check.q: Why do guests at langar traditionally sit on the floor together?
choices: because chairs are forbidden in all religions
to show the Khalsa is secret
so no one sits higher than another
check.why: Sitting together on the floor shows the Sikh teaching of equality.

check.q: Which is one of the five Ks?
check.why: The kara is one of the five Ks; karma, kami and koan belong to other traditions.

lessons.title: Mahavira and Ahimsa
lessons.mainIdea: Jains follow the teaching of Mahavira and the earlier Tirthankaras, which centers on ahimsa, doing no harm to any living being.
reading: A Jain nun walks slowly, gently sweeping the ground ahead with a soft broom so she will not step on an insect. Some Jain monks and nuns cover their mouths with a cloth. These acts show *ahimsa*, the principle of non-harm to any living thing. Jains teach that every living being, even a tiny insect, has a soul, called a jiva.

Jains honor 24 *Tirthankaras*, teachers who crossed over the river of rebirth and showed others the way. The 24th is Mahavira, who lived in northern India around the same time as the Buddha, often dated to the 6th or 5th century BCE. Jain tradition says he left home at about 30, lived as a wandering ascetic and reached perfect knowledge.

Like Hindus and Buddhists, Jains speak of karma and rebirth. But in Jain teaching, karma is a fine substance that sticks to the soul when a person acts with harm or desire. Careful, nonviolent living removes it. The goal is liberation, when the soul is free of karma. Most Jains live in India today, and Jain temples also stand in the Chicago suburbs.

words.d: non-harm; the principle of not hurting any living being
in Jainism, one of 24 teachers who showed the way across the cycle of rebirth
in Jainism, the soul found in every living being

look.title: All Beings Love Life
look.text: All beings are fond of life. They like pleasure and dislike pain. They shun destruction and wish to live. To all, life is dear. So one should not kill, harm or cause suffering to any living creature.
look.cite: Acaranga Sutra, Book 1 (a Jain scripture; see the translation by Hermann Jacobi, 1884), paraphrase
look.prompt: What reason does this passage give for ahimsa? How might it shape what a Jain family eats?

check.q: What does ahimsa mean?
check.why: Ahimsa is non-harm, central to Jainism. Respect for parents is xiao, a Confucian idea.

check.q: Who was Mahavira?
check.why: Jains honor Mahavira as the 24th Tirthankara.

check.q: How is karma described differently in Jainism?
choices: as a fine substance that sticks to the soul
as a kind of shrine gate
check.why: Jain teaching describes karma as a subtle substance that binds the soul.

lessons.title: The Jain Vows
lessons.mainIdea: Jains take vows of non-harm, truth, not stealing, self-control and non-attachment; monks and nuns keep them strictly and lay people in a milder form.
reading: Jains organize their way of life around five *vows*. They are ahimsa (non-harm), satya (truthfulness), asteya (not stealing), brahmacharya (self-control, especially in sexual life) and aparigraha (*non-attachment* to possessions). Monks and nuns take these as great vows and keep them strictly. Lay Jains take them as smaller vows suited to family life.

The vows shape daily choices. Jains are vegetarian, and many avoid root vegetables such as onions and potatoes, since pulling them up kills the whole plant and many tiny beings in the soil. Many Jains do not eat after sunset. Jain businesses often avoid trades that cause great harm to living things.

Jains practice anekantavada, the teaching of many-sidedness. It holds that truth is complex and any one view sees only part of it. Jains tell the story of blind men who each touch one part of an elephant and describe it differently. Jains are divided into two main groups, the Digambara and the Shvetambara, which differ on practices such as monks' clothing.

words.d: a serious promise to live in a certain way
not clinging to possessions or desires
the Jain teaching that truth has many sides

look.title: A Jain Menu
look.text: A school cafeteria offers: a chicken sandwich, a potato soup, rice with lentils, an onion salad and fresh fruit. A Jain student who keeps her family's customs looks at the tray line at lunch.
look.prompt: Which foods would she most likely choose? Explain each choice using ahimsa and the vows.

check.q: Why do many Jains avoid root vegetables?
choices: pulling them up kills the plant and many tiny beings
check.why: Out of ahimsa, many Jains avoid roots because harvesting them destroys the whole plant and small life.

check.q: What is aparigraha?
check.why: Aparigraha, non-attachment, is one of the five Jain vows.

check.q: What does the story of the blind men and the elephant illustrate?
choices: anekantavada, that truth has many sides
check.why: Jains use the elephant story to explain anekantavada, many-sidedness.

lessons.title: Confucius and Ren
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught that people become truly good through ren, humane care for others, practiced in everyday relationships.
reading: Confucius, called Kongzi in Chinese, lived in China from about 551 to 479 BCE, according to tradition. It was a time of war between rival states. He worked as a teacher and adviser, hoping rulers would govern by good example instead of force. After his death, his students collected his sayings in the *Analects*.

The central virtue in the Analects is *ren*, often translated as humaneness or goodness. Ren means caring for others and treating them well. Confucius taught that a person grows in ren through practice, starting with family and moving outward to the community and the state. He called a person of great virtue a junzi, an exemplary or noble person.

Scholars debate whether Confucianism is best called a religion, a philosophy or a way of life. Confucius spoke of Heaven, or tian, and honored ancestral rites. Yet he said little about gods or life after death. In China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, Confucian ideas have shaped families, schools and government for more than two thousand years.

words.d: the collected sayings of Confucius, gathered by his students
humaneness or goodness; caring for others
in Confucian teaching, an exemplary person of great virtue

look.title: One Word for a Whole Life
look.text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, 'Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.'
look.cite: Analects 15.23, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (1861)
look.prompt: What does reciprocity mean in this saying? Give an example of it from a school day.

check.q: What is the Analects?
check.why: Confucius's students collected his sayings in the Analects.

check.q: What is ren?
check.why: Ren is the central Confucian virtue of humaneness; wu wei is Daoist.

check.q: According to Analects 15.23, what should you not do to others?
choices: what you do not want done to yourself
check.why: Confucius names reciprocity: do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.

lessons.title: Li and Xiao
lessons.mainIdea: Confucian teaching holds that proper conduct, li, and devotion to parents, xiao, build harmony in families and in society.
reading: At a Chinese family dinner, grandparents are served first. The children greet each elder by name before eating. On the Qingming Festival in spring, many families sweep the graves of their ancestors and bring food and flowers. Confucian tradition sees these customs as more than politeness. They express *li*, proper conduct and ritual.

Li includes ceremonies, like honoring ancestors, and everyday manners, like bowing or greeting elders. Confucius taught that practicing li with a sincere heart shapes a person's character. He thought outer actions and inner feelings belong together. Li without ren, he warned, is empty.

One of the most important Confucian virtues is *xiao*, or filial piety, which means devotion and respect toward one's parents. Confucian teaching describes five key relationships: ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, older and younger sibling, and friend and friend. Each side has duties. Critics, then and now, have debated how these roles treat women and younger people.

words.d: in Confucian teaching, proper conduct, ritual and good manners
filial piety; devotion and respect toward one's parents
a family member from long ago, such as a great-grandparent

look.title: More Than Feeding Parents
look.text: A student asked about filial piety. Confucius answered that people today think it means only providing food for their parents. But even dogs and horses are given food. Without reverence, he asked, what is the difference?
look.prompt: According to Confucius, what must go along with caring for parents' needs? How does this saying connect li and ren?

check.q: What is xiao?
choices: devotion and respect toward one's parents
check.why: Xiao is filial piety, a key Confucian virtue.

check.q: What did Confucius teach about li without ren?
check.why: Confucius taught that outer ritual needs inner humaneness to have meaning.

check.q: Families sweep their ancestors' graves at Qingming. Which Confucian idea does this show?
check.why: Honoring ancestors expresses filial piety (xiao) through ritual (li).

lessons.title: The Examinations
lessons.mainIdea: For about 1,300 years, China chose many officials through exams on the Confucian classics.
reading: Imagine a young man in a tiny exam cell, one of thousands in a row. For days, he writes essays about Confucian texts that he has memorized since childhood. If he passes the highest level, his whole family rises in honor. This was the Chinese *civil-service examination* system.

The exams began under the Sui dynasty, around 605 CE. They grew larger under the Tang and Song dynasties. Candidates studied the Confucian classics, including the Analects. The idea was that officials should be chosen for learning and virtue, not only for noble birth. In practice, families with money for tutors had a great advantage, and women could not take the exams.

The system lasted until 1905, when the Qing government ended it. Through the exams, Confucian values shaped China's government and schools for centuries. Korea and Vietnam adopted similar exams. Today, many people in East Asia still link hard study and respect for teachers with Confucian tradition.

words.d: a test used to choose government officials; in China, based on the Confucian classics
a line of rulers from the same family

look.title: The Exams Through Time
look.cite: Standard dates in histories of imperial China
look.prompt: About how many years did the exam system last? What does that long span suggest about Confucian influence?

check.q: What did candidates study for China's exams?
check.why: The exams tested knowledge of Confucian texts such as the Analects.

check.q: When did the exam system end?
check.why: The Qing government ended the exams in 1905; 605 CE is roughly when they began.

check.q: Which group could NOT take the exams?
check.why: Women were barred from the exams; in principle many men could try, though wealth helped.

sections.title: The Dao, the Kami and Blending

lessons.title: Laozi and the Dao
lessons.mainIdea: Daoists seek harmony with the Dao, the natural way of all things, through simplicity, balance and wu wei.
reading: In a Chinese park at dawn, people move slowly through the gentle motions of tai chi. Many practitioners say the practice helps them feel balanced, like water flowing. This image of flowing water appears again and again in the *Daodejing*, a short book of poems traditionally credited to Laozi. Scholars debate whether Laozi was a real person. Many date the book to about the 4th century BCE.

The Daodejing opens by saying that the Dao that can be spoken of is not the lasting Dao. *Dao* means the way. Daoists describe it as the natural way of all things, beyond words. They teach *wu wei*, often translated as effortless action. Wu wei means acting in harmony with nature, without forcing things, like water that flows around a rock.

Daoists also speak of *yin and yang*, two opposite forces that complete each other, like dark and light or rest and motion. Religious Daoism grew later, with temples, priests, rituals and many deities, and a hope for long life. Daoism and Confucianism often balanced each other in China: one stressing duties in society, the other harmony with nature.

words.d: the way; in Daoism, the natural way of all things
the short classic of Daoism, traditionally credited to Laozi
effortless action; acting in harmony with nature without forcing
two opposite forces that complete and balance each other

look.title: Like Water
look.text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 8, trans. James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)
look.prompt: Why might the Daodejing praise water? How does water show wu wei?

check.q: What does Dao mean?
check.why: Dao means the way, the natural way of all things.

check.q: Which example best shows wu wei?
choices: a soldier forcing open a gate
a student memorizing for an exam
check.why: Wu wei is effortless action, like water that does not force its way.

check.q: How did Daoism often balance Confucianism in China?
choices: Daoism stressed harmony with nature; Confucianism stressed duties in society
they taught exactly the same thing
check.why: Confucian teaching centers on social roles; Daoism centers on the natural way.

lessons.title: Shinto: Kami and Shrines
lessons.mainIdea: Shinto, the traditional religion of Japan, honors the kami, sacred powers found in nature, ancestors and special places.
reading: A huge old tree at a Japanese shrine has a thick straw rope tied around it, hung with white paper zigzags. The rope, called shimenawa, marks the tree as a sacred place. In *Shinto*, Japan's traditional religion, such places are homes of the *kami*. Kami are sacred powers or spirits found in mountains, rivers, trees, ancestors and people of great virtue.

Shinto has no single founder and no single scripture. Its ancient stories are recorded in the Kojiki, compiled in 712 CE. It teaches purity and gratitude. Worshipers wash their hands at the shrine and bow. The *torii* gate marks the step from ordinary space into sacred space. The Grand Shrine at Ise, dedicated to the sun kami Amaterasu, is Shinto's most honored shrine.

Many Shinto customs mark the seasons and the stages of life. Families bring newborns to a shrine. On Shichi-Go-San, children ages three, five and seven visit a shrine in bright clothes. Festivals called matsuri carry the kami through the streets in portable shrines. Many Japanese people say they take part in Shinto customs as tradition more than as belief.

words.d: the traditional religion of Japan, centered on the kami
in Shinto, sacred powers or spirits in nature, ancestors and places
a gate that marks the entrance to a Shinto shrine

look.title: Crossing the Gate
look.text: A visitor walks under a torii, stops at a stone basin, rinses her hands and mouth, then approaches the shrine. She rings a bell, bows twice, claps twice and bows again. A rope with white paper zigzags hangs above the entrance.
look.prompt: Explain each step using Shinto ideas of purity, respect and sacred space.

check.q: What are kami?
choices: sacred powers found in nature, ancestors and places
check.why: In Shinto, kami are sacred powers or spirits.

check.q: What does a torii mark?
choices: the end of the exam system
the entrance to a Shinto shrine
check.why: The torii gate marks the passage into sacred space at a shrine.

check.q: Why do worshipers rinse their hands at a Shinto shrine?
choices: Shinto stresses purity before approaching the kami
check.why: Purification is central to Shinto shrine visits.

lessons.title: Three Teachings and Two Ways
lessons.mainIdea: In China and Japan, many people blend several traditions, which makes simple religious labels hard to apply.
reading: In a Chinese home, a family might keep a tablet honoring ancestors, a Confucian practice. On a holiday they might visit a Daoist temple to ask for good fortune. For a funeral they might invite Buddhist monks to chant. In China these are often called the *Three Teachings*: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. Many people draw on all three.

In Japan, Buddhism arrived from Korea in the 6th century CE. Over time, Buddhism and Shinto blended closely. Some Buddhists taught that the kami were local forms of Buddhas. Temples and shrines often stood side by side. In 1868, the Meiji government ordered Shinto and Buddhism to be officially separated. Even so, many families still take part in both, as the Satos did.

This *syncretism*, or blending of traditions, makes counting adherents hard. A survey question like What is your religion? may not fit someone who follows several ways. Scholars say it is more accurate to describe what people practice than to fit them into one box. Chicago's Chinatown and its Japanese American communities show some of these blended customs today.

words.d: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, as they are often combined in China
the blending of beliefs and practices from different traditions

look.title: Which Box to Check?
look.text: A survey asks a woman in Japan to choose one religion. She visits a shrine at New Year, was married in a Shinto ceremony, keeps a Buddhist altar for her parents and hopes to have a Buddhist funeral. She says she is not very religious.
look.prompt: What box should she check? Explain why surveys can give confusing numbers for places where people blend traditions.

check.q: Which three traditions make up China's Three Teachings?
check.why: The Three Teachings are Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism.

check.q: What is syncretism?
choices: the blending of beliefs and practices from different traditions
check.why: Syncretism means blending traditions, as in Japan's mix of Shinto and Buddhism.

check.q: What happened in Japan in 1868?
choices: the government ordered Shinto and Buddhism separated
check.why: The Meiji government separated Shinto and Buddhism officially in 1868.

review.q: Who was the first Sikh Guru?
review.why: Guru Nanak, born in 1469, was the first Sikh Guru; Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth.

review.q: Which Sikh practice shows the equality of all people through a shared meal?
review.why: At langar, everyone eats together, sitting as equals.

review.q: Which tradition centers its whole way of life on ahimsa and five vows?
review.why: Jains build their way of life on ahimsa and the five vows.

review.q: Which Confucian virtue means devotion to parents?
review.why: Xiao is filial piety; ren is humaneness.

review.q: Which text begins by saying the Dao that can be spoken of is not the lasting Dao?
review.why: This is the opening of the Daodejing, the Daoist classic.

review.q: In Shinto, where are kami believed to dwell?
choices: in nature, ancestors and special places
review.why: Shinto teaches that kami are found in mountains, trees, ancestors and places.

review.q: What did Confucius say about reciprocity in Analects 15.23?
choices: do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself
review.why: This is Confucius's rule of reciprocity; the others are Daoist, Jain and Sikh ideas.

review.q: Why is it hard to count followers of religions in Japan?
choices: many people take part in both Shinto and Buddhism
review.why: Blending traditions means one person may follow both Shinto and Buddhist customs.
